podcast.body: A reunion album with producer Nile Rogers, intended to remind listeners of David Bowie's debonair 80s image. However, it arrived in a changed pop landscape where R&B was new Jack Swing and top 40 radio favored club music and alt pop, leaving only alternative rock stations hospitable to Bowie. Despite upbeat reviews and its lead single "Jump They Say" reaching number 5 on the modern rock chart, poor distribution and promotion led to the album barely scraping the top 40 and becoming his shortest-lived album on the Billboard 200 to that date. "David and Nile's 1993 reunion was called Black Tie White Noise, an attempt to remind listeners of David Bowie's debonair 80s image."

podcast.body: This album, released after Bowie had resolved his legal issues with a former manager and was free to make music on his own terms, was generally acknowledged as his best work since "Scary Monsters" thirteen years earlier. Despite its critical reception, it did not produce any hit singles. "In 1993, a record called Black Tie White Noise didn't result in any hit singles, but it was generally acknowledged to be his best works in Scary Monsters 13 years earlier."
